panels.heading: Hi, this is ==Huq== — better known as ==Panda== among friends.
body: They started calling me that partly for the size, but mostly because I’m the calmest guy in the room when everything’s on fire. *(Haters gonna call it couch-potato energy!)*

Off the clock, I’m a late-night chef, an anime-and-series binger, and the friend who sends you memes at 2 AM. I draw cartoons, capture moments on my phone, and I’m a recovering procrastinator who somehow always ships on time.

papers.title: ‘Khep’: Exploring Factors that Influence the Preference of Contractual Rides to Ride-Sharing Apps in Bangladesh
papers.authors: A. B. Alok, H. Sakib, S. A. Ullah, **F. Huq**, R. Ghosh, J. J. Mondal, M. S. I. Sakif, J. Noor
papers.line: Why riders cut the app and haggle with the driver instead.
papers.proceedings: Proceedings of the 6th ACM SIGCAS/SIGCHI Conference on Computing and Sustainable Societies (COMPASS ’23)
papers.abstract: With rapid urbanization and increasing traffic congestion in major cities, alternative modes of transportation have gained significant attention. The ride-sharing app revolution also has sparked a significant transformation in the transportation industry, along with “Khep”, an unusual ride-sharing approach where individuals negotiate fares directly with drivers personally, which has become a popular means of transportation. In this research, we investigate various factors that influence the preference for such unconventional contractual rides over ride-sharing apps, such as cultural norms, trust issues, affordability, and accessibility. Moreover, we explore the role of technology literacy, marketing strategies, and regulatory frameworks in shaping the adoption landscape. After conducting a survey and interviews, we conduct a thorough analysis to determine the expected findings and uncover meaningful insights regarding the utilization, preferences, and challenges within the ride-sharing industry in Bangladesh. The findings of this study reveal that cultural factors, such as the preference for bargaining and personal connections, strongly influence the popularity of contractual rides. Additionally, concerns related to safety, data privacy, and trust act as barriers to ride-sharing app adoption. Being associated with UN SDG Goals 11 and 9, the implications of this research extend beyond Bangladesh and can provide insights for policymakers, transportation companies, and technology developers seeking to understand the factors shaping the adoption of ride-sharing apps in similar contexts.
findings: Bargaining culture and personal connections make “khep” rides popular.
Safety, data-privacy and trust concerns hold back ride-sharing app adoption.
Linked to UN SDGs 9 and 11, with lessons beyond Bangladesh.

papers.title: Navigating Truth in the Sea of Content: Exploring Influential Factors Shaping User Perceptions of Trustworthiness in YouTube Content
papers.authors: A. B. Alok, **F. Huq**, S. A. Ullah, R. Ghosh, J. Noor
papers.line: What makes people trust a YouTube video, or scroll past it.
papers.proceedings: Proceedings of the 7th ACM SIGCAS/SIGCHI Conference on Computing and Sustainable Societies (COMPASS ’24)
papers.abstract: In today’s digital age, YouTube stands as a vital hub for information across various domains, from entertainment to education. However, the persistent challenge of misinformation threatens its integrity. This study explores the complex dynamics of trust and legitimacy within YouTube’s content ecosystem, uncovering factors shaping user perceptions in Bangladesh. We highlight the crucial roles of creator reputation, content presentation, and social validation in building trust while emphasizing the need to address misleading content effectively. Employing a mixed-methods approach, we conducted surveys (n=71) and interviews (n=19) to gain insights into user experiences comprehensively. By addressing gaps in current research, our study contributes to the HCI and ICT4D communities, illuminating critical issues in the digital realm. As YouTube continues to influence our online landscape, grasping trust and misinformation becomes essential for fostering an informed and trustworthy online community.
findings: Creator reputation is the strongest signal of trust.
Presentation and social validation (views, likes, comments) shape credibility.
Misleading content must be tackled to keep the platform trustworthy.

papers.title: Comprehensive Insights into the ‘Khep’ Phenomenon: Understanding the Full Spectrum from Companies to Commuters in Transforming Gig of Ride-Sharing
papers.authors: A. B. Alok, **F. Huq**, S. A. Ullah, R. Ghosh, H. Sakib, J. Noor
papers.line: The journal follow-up: both sides of the ride, companies and commuters.
papers.proceedings: ACM Journal on Computing and Sustainable Societies, Vol. 3, Issue 3
papers.abstract: In the face of escalating urbanization and traffic congestion, the emergence of ride-sharing applications has triggered a transformative shift in transportation and the gig economy, with “khep” (a new form of contractual rides) emerging as a distinctive and popular ride-sharing phenomenon in Bangladesh. Having a lack of prior research on “khep” phenomenon in the context of HCI and ICT4D, we conduct comprehensive research involving a two-phase data collection to unravel the intricacies of khep. We present the context from the perspectives of both companies and commuters, examining factors influencing the preference for contractual rides over conventional ride-sharing apps. Cultural norms, trust dynamics, affordability, and accessibility are scrutinized alongside the role of technology literacy, marketing strategies, and regulatory frameworks in shaping the adoption landscape. Through a blend of surveys and interviews in each phase, the study provides nuanced insights into utilization patterns, preferences, and challenges within the Bangladeshi ride-sharing industry, with a specific focus on the khep phenomenon. Aligned with HCI labor work, the study’s implications transcend Bangladesh, offering valuable insights for ICT4D and HCI researchers, policymakers, transportation companies, and technology developers seeking a holistic understanding of the factors shaping the preference for contractual rides within the unique context of the khep phenomenon.
findings: Looks at both sides of khep: ride-sharing companies and commuters.
Cultural norms, trust, affordability and access drive the choice of contractual rides.
Tech literacy, marketing and regulation shape how the apps get adopted.

items.title: CMP Fingerprint Matching Software
items.tagline: AI-assisted fingerprint records, crime scene matching and suspect verification for the Corps of Military Police.

sections.heading: The problem
sections.body: Comparing fingerprints by hand is slow and error-prone. CMP needed one system to keep fingerprint records, find matches for crime scene evidence, and confirm a suspect’s identity.

sections.heading: The solution
points: **Fingerprint records:** a central database of prints from individuals with prior offences and other persons of interest.
**Crime scene matching:** latent prints lifted from a crime scene are searched against the database to find likely matches.
**Suspect verification:** a match is confirmed by comparing it with prints taken from the suspect.

sections.heading: My role
points: Defined the system requirements for all three functions with the client.
Researched AI models for fingerprint matching and helped choose the approach.
Designed the workflow from fingerprint input to verified result.

sections.heading: Challenge
points: **Getting better results from the AI models:** out-of-the-box accuracy wasn’t good enough, so the models had to be tweaked and re-tested repeatedly to improve matching results.

sections.heading: Results
points: Delivered fingerprint storage, matching and verification software for PC and web.
Replaced manual comparison with AI-assisted matching.

items.title: Brand Review.AI
items.tagline: Checking designs against brand guidelines automatically with AI.

sections.heading: The problem
sections.body: Checking every design against brand and event guidelines by hand is slow, and small mistakes in colours, fonts or visuals slip through.

sections.heading: The solution
sections.body: A web tool that uses AI to review a design and flag where it breaks the guidelines, covering:
points: **Colours:** off-brand shades and palettes.
**Fonts:** wrong typefaces or styles.
**Visuals:** imagery and layout that don’t follow the rules.

sections.heading: My role
points: Researched AI models for design analysis.
Flagged technical risks early and proposed fixes.
Coordinated delivery and client communication.

sections.heading: Challenge
points: **Reliable AI judgment:** guidelines are often subjective, so the models had to be tested to give consistent, useful feedback rather than false alarms.

sections.heading: Results
points: Delivered a web tool that automates brand compliance checks.
Faster reviews, with fewer off-brand designs reaching publication.

items.title: Combine Harvester Simulator
items.tagline: Training combine harvester operators safely, without a real machine.

sections.heading: The problem
sections.body: Operators learn on real harvesters: risky, costly in fuel and wear, and only possible at harvest time. The client needed a simulator real enough for skills to carry over.

sections.heading: My role
points: Turned training goals into documented software requirements.
Ran daily Scrum and sprints in Jira and GitHub Projects; main client contact.
Tested every build on the physical rig before release.

sections.heading: Approach and challenges
points: **Defined “realistic”** as testable requirements, reviewed with the client each sprint.
**Built hardware and software in parallel** against a shared list of control signals.
**Shipped a playable build every sprint** so issues were caught early.
**Used client experts’ knowledge**, documented so the whole team shared it.

sections.heading: Results
points: Risk-free operator training on a working hardware simulator.
Lower training costs and year-round practice.
The process carried over to our Unilever truck and GIZ VR safety simulators.

items.title: TechVital VR Medical Equipment Showcase
items.tagline: Showing a full range of medical equipment without a trip to the warehouse.

sections.heading: The problem
sections.body: Medical equipment is large, expensive and hard to move. To see the full product range, TechVital’s clients had to visit a warehouse or factory, and even then they couldn’t look inside a machine.

sections.heading: The solution
sections.body: A VR showroom on Meta Quest 3 where clients can:
points: **Browse every product type** in one place, anywhere.
**View each machine in 360°**, in full detail.
**Take equipment apart part by part** and inspect each component separately.

sections.heading: My role
points: Coordinated end-to-end delivery; main client contact.
Turned the product range into requirements: which equipment, which parts, which details to show.
Tested every build before the showcase.

sections.heading: Results
points: Delivered **Bangladesh’s first VR healthcare showcase**.
Clients explore the whole range, inside and out, without a warehouse or factory visit.
Brochures replaced by interactive 3D demos.

items.title: Unilever Truck Driving Simulator
items.tagline: Training Unilever’s truck drivers on a realistic simulator before they hit the road.

meta.v: Unity, C#, steering wheel and pedal rig

sections.heading: The problem
sections.body: Unilever needed a real-life truck driving simulator for driver training. It had to drive like a real truck and enforce strict road safety rules and company driving policies, all on a short timeline.

sections.heading: My role
points: Designed the product and planned the delivery for a cross-functional team of 8.
Main client contact: gathered and managed the safety and policy requirements.
Ran daily Scrum and tracked work in Jira and GitHub Projects.

sections.heading: Challenges
points: **Short timeline, heavy detail:** a long list of requirements had to be prioritised and tracked closely to fit the deadline.
**Realistic truck physics:** steering, braking and handling had to feel like a real truck on the wheel and pedal rig.
**Extensive safety and policy rules:** road safety standards and Unilever’s own driving policies had to be built into the simulator.

sections.heading: Results
points: Delivered a working **truck driving simulator** for Unilever driver training.
Drivers practise safe driving and company policy without risk on real roads.
